column1: Text-Based Forecasting of Inflation with arXiv News Data

The thesis titled Inflation  Unemployment  and Labor Force: Phillips Curves and Long-Term Projections for Japan by Oleg I. Kitov and Ivan O. Kitov explores the relationship between inflation  unemployment  and labor force changes in Japan using the Phillips curve framework. Initially estimated for the period from 1980 to 2003  the models have been updated with data through 2012. The study confirms the Phillips curve's concept that rising unemployment leads to decreasing inflation and extends this by linking both inflation and unemployment to changes in the labor force. The updated models accurately describe Japan's disinflation in the 1980s and 1990s and the deflationary period starting in the late 1990s. The authors predict a long-term deflationary trend in Japan  with the GDP deflator expected to remain negative over the next 40 years  and unemployment rising from 4.3% in 2012 to 5.5% by 2050.

The introduction revisits empirical relationships between inflation  unemployment  and labor force changes within the Phillips curve framework. The original Phillips curve  formulated by Phillips in 1958  and the reverse causation direction introduced by Fisher in 1926  consider the link between inflation and unemployment as causal. The authors first estimated this causal relationship in 2006 and now test its performance with new data. They extend the standard Phillips curve by incorporating the labor force change rate  a variable not previously tested as a predictor of inflation and unemployment. The re-estimated relationships confirm the original models  suggesting limited control over inflation and unemployment by monetary and fiscal authorities. The 2007 economic crisis  which altered economic activity parameters without significantly affecting inflation  questions central banks' ability to influence these variables through monetary policy. The study suggests that Japan's shrinking labor force will lead to long-term deflation and higher unemployment.

The paper discusses other studies with differing views. Leigh (2004) examined Japan's monetary policy and liquidity trap  concluding that aggressive responses to inflation gaps would not have significantly improved economic performance. This aligns with the authors' findings that inflation is influenced by labor force and unemployment rather than monetary policy. Nelson (2006) argued that recognizing inflation as a monetary phenomenon allows central banks to control it  but the authors' model suggests otherwise. De Veirman (2007) and Kamada (2004) studied the output-inflation trade-off and output gap's role in inflation prediction  respectively  but the authors' model attributes deflation to labor force changes  not output gaps. Sekine (2001) and Feyzioğlu and Willard (2006) found limited improvement in inflation forecasts with additional variables  supporting the authors' focus on labor force dependence.

Unemployment in Japan has also been studied outside the Phillips curve framework. Caporale and Gil-Alana (2006) identified a structural break in Japanese unemployment around 1993  while Pascalau (2007) found a long-run equilibrium relation between unemployment  productivity  and real wages. Kitov (2006) estimated empirical coefficients for various Phillips curve representations in Japan  using a simplified boundary element method and LSQ technique. The model found a slope of 1.77 and a constant term of -0.0035 for CPI inflation and labor force  with labor force changes occurring almost simultaneously with inflation changes.
